one_line: Public-prefixed env vars (NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_, PUBLIC_) ship into the client bundle, so a private Supabase key behind one leaks to every visitor; the fix is server-side calls, bundle checks and CI guardrails.
summary: A short Better Stack explainer on how private Supabase keys end up in front-end JavaScript. It cites a report that scanned about 20,000 indie apps and found one in nine exposing Supabase credentials in client code. The speaker explains that build tools inline any variable with a public prefix (Next.js, Vite, SvelteKit) into the client bundle, and that anon/publishable keys are meant to be public while service-role/secret keys bypass row-level security. A demo builds a small Next.js CRUD app with a private key behind NEXT_PUBLIC_, then finds it by searching the compiled bundle. The fix is to have the browser call its own server-side API, which holds the private key, then rebuild and confirm the key is gone. Guardrails proposed are CI secret scanning, a PR rule treating public-prefixed variables as public, and key rotation on any suspicion of exposure.

key_ideas.idea: A public-prefixed env var is a shipping label, not a safety label
key_ideas.detail: NEXT_PUBLIC_ (Next.js), VITE_ (Vite) and PUBLIC_ (SvelteKit) tell the build tool to inline the value into the client JavaScript bundle, so any visitor can download it.

key_ideas.idea: Supabase keys split into public and private classes
key_ideas.detail: The anon/publishable key is designed to be visible. The service-role/secret key bypasses row-level security, so if it reaches the browser, RLS policies stop mattering.

key_ideas.idea: The leak is an accident, not a hack
key_ideas.detail: The speaker's point is that the affected apps were not breached; the credentials were simply in the public JS that the app serves, readable by anyone who opens DevTools.

key_ideas.idea: Reproduction: one private key behind a public prefix is enough
key_ideas.detail: Demo: a Next.js CRUD app linked to Supabase, a private key placed behind NEXT_PUBLIC_, a production build, then a search of the compiled bundle that finds both the URL and the key.

key_ideas.idea: Fix by moving privileged calls to the server
key_ideas.detail: The browser calls the app's own API route or server function; that server-side code holds the private key and calls Supabase. Rebuild and search the bundle again to confirm the key is gone.

key_ideas.idea: Fixing the key is not the whole job
key_ideas.detail: Also enable RLS on user-facing tables, verify the policies do what you think, and test them, since the speaker says this step is often skipped.

key_ideas.idea: Guardrails stop the regression during a rushed release
key_ideas.detail: Add secret scanning in CI so builds fail when a key appears where it should not, add a PR rule that treats public-prefixed variables as public by default, and rotate keys on any hint of exposure rather than waiting.

techniques.name: Audit the shipped build for secrets
techniques.how: Build the app the way you ship it (the speaker runs npm run build), then search the output for Supabase, JWT, service, secret, and anything token-shaped. The video shows searching the compiled JS in Chrome DevTools; it does not name a build output directory. Treat any private-looking hit as compromised: rotate it and move the logic server-side.
techniques.when: Before each release, and after adding or renaming any env var that uses a public prefix.

techniques.name: Proxy privileged calls through your own server
techniques.how: Keep the service-role or secret key out of client code. The browser calls an app-owned API route or server function; that server code holds the private key and calls Supabase. Rebuild and confirm the key is absent from the bundle.
techniques.when: Any operation that needs a private Supabase key (admin writes, RLS-bypassing reads) from a browser-facing app.

techniques.name: Enable and test RLS on user-facing tables
techniques.how: Turn on row-level security for every user-facing table and check that each policy does what it is meant to do by testing it, not just reading it.
techniques.when: Alongside any Supabase key change, since RLS is the backstop for the public anon key.

techniques.name: Review rule for public-prefixed variables
techniques.how: In PR review, treat anything named NEXT_PUBLIC_, VITE_ or PUBLIC_ as public by default and question any secret placed behind those prefixes.
techniques.when: Any PR that adds or changes environment variables in a front-end project.

techniques.name: CI secret scanning as a build gate
techniques.how: Run a secret scanner in the pipeline so the build fails when a key appears in a place it should not. The video names no specific scanner.
techniques.when: Every build pipeline that ships a browser bundle.

techniques.name: Rotate on suspicion
techniques.how: If there is even a slight hint that a key was exposed, rotate it instead of waiting to see whether it is abused.
techniques.when: Any private key found in a bundle, log, or repo.

numbers.claim: Report scanned about 20,000 indie apps; one in nine exposed Supabase credentials in front-end code
Demo video length is about 4 minutes 16 seconds (the whole video)

hot_takes: The one-in-nine figure is attributed only to an unnamed report from 'this month'; the video gives no methodology, and the speaker never names the source.
The core message is simple and correct: if a key is in the bundle, it is public. The video is thin on specifics beyond that (no CI tool named, no RLS policy examples).

relevance.why: AgentOS has a security-guardrails pillar (L1 PII/prompt-injection scan, L2C exec-gate). This video is about secret placement in client bundles, which is adjacent but not core.
relevance.action: If AgentOS ever ships a browser-side UI, add a CI step that fails the build when provider or service keys appear in the built JS.

relevance.why: ProsHarness emphasises zero-token credential handling. The video's rule that private keys stay server-side fits that principle.
relevance.action: Apply the bundle-grep check to any browser-facing ProsHarness UI so credentials are not inlined into client assets.

relevance.why: Common failure mode for any team shipping a browser app with a backend service key, and cheap to guard against.
relevance.action: Add a secret-scanning step to CI and a grep of the production build output for private-key patterns before release.
